riscos.descricao: O arquivo de testes contém grande proporção de conteúdo redundante que distrai o modelo da localização do defeito, com queda de RSR em parte dos modelos.
Descrições nativas ambíguas do QuixBugs podem levar modelos de alta capacidade (por exemplo, DeepseekV3.2) a modificar código não central, causando quedas de RSR.
Em modelos de baixa capacidade, informação redundante causa sobrecarga de contexto e dispersão de atenção, reduzindo a RSR das combinações (efeito inibitório).
Limitação de generalização apresentada pelo estudo: conjunto pequeno (40 casos) e idealizado do QuixBugs, sem projetos grandes nem erros de sintaxe, e apenas seis modelos testados.

Diretriz prática: usar o TestFile só em combinação com TestOutput, em modelos comerciais, após limpeza de redundância; a limpeza de redundância não foi executada nem avaliada.

citacoes.trecho: Experimental results reveal that code description and BuggyLine are universal high-value information for all models, while PDG and TestOutput only benefit high-capability models, and TestFile acts as low-value noise with inhibitory effects in most cases.

High-capability commercial models exhibit significant synergistic effects with full-information combinations, achieving a maximum Repair Success Rate (RSR) of 97.5%, while low-capability models suffer from context overload due to redundant information.
BuggyCode: Directly extract the buggy code from the QuixBugs dataset with comment sections removed, as illustrated in Fig. 2.
Description: For each Python buggy code snippet in the QuixBugs dataset, a functional description of the code is provided immediately after the code block, as shown in Fig. 2.
BuggyLine: QuixBugs provides both buggy and correct versions of the code; the BuggyLine is identified by comparing these two versions.
PDG (Program Dependence Graph): Encompasses data dependencies and control dependencies associated with the buggy line within the target function.
TestFile: The test file corresponding to the buggy code in the QuixBugs dataset.

TestOutput: Execution results of buggy code from test file runs, autocapturing error-containing test logs with key info like test case pass/fail status, input parameters, expected/actual outputs and error code lines (e.g. for bucketsort in Quixbugs: “6 failed, 1 passed”, “input_data = [[8,5,3,1,9,6, …],10], expected = [0,1,2,3,4,5, …]”, “test_bucketsort.py:26: AssertionError”).
Evaluate the independent impact of each auxiliary information type on repair performance, identifying high-value and low-value information.
1 Test-related combination: BuggyCode + TestFile + TestOutput, integrate test-related information to explore the synergistic effect of test feedback (TestOutput) and test logic (TestFile) on repair.

1 Full-information combination: BuggyCode + Description + BuggyLine + PDG + TestFile + TestOutput, include all 6 information types to explore the upper limit of information integration and potential inhibitory effects between information.
To ensure that all LLMs follow the same repair constraints and output format, we design a unified Prompt template, which is divided into system prompts and task prompts:

You are a senior Python development expert, proficient in code debugging and bug fixing, especially in resolving Python semantic errors and runtime errors caused by logical flaws (e.g., incorrect loop conditions, wrong variable assignments).
1. Only return the fixed pure Python core code, without any additional content;
Single information enhancement scenario: Insert the corresponding auxiliary information into the prompt.

Combined information scenario: Arrange the information in the order of “ BuggyCode → TestFile → TestOutput” or “BuggyCode → Description → BuggyLine → PDG → TestFile → TestOutput” to ensure the logical coherence of the prompt and avoid information confusion.
Call each LLM with the Prompt, obtain the generated patch.
Execute the test case on the patch to verify whether it passes all tests; if passed, mark it as a successful repair.
Evaluation Metrics: Core metric: Repair Success Rate (RSR) = (Number of successfully repaired test cases / Total number of test cases) × 100%.

All base-lines are evaluated on the same QuixBugs Python subset (40 bugs) to ensure fair comparison, with the core metric being the Repair Success Rate (RSR) of our models versus the baselines under this consistent dataset.
Ambiguous native descriptions in QuixBugs may mislead high-capability models (e.g., DeepseekV3.2) to modify non-core code, causing temporary RSR drops.
Core reason: Test files contain a large proportion of redundant content, with valid test logic making up only a small fraction, which distracts models from defect localization.
Inhibitory mechanism: Low-capability models lack information weight assignment capabilities, leading to context overload and attention dispersion from redundant information.
Notably, CodeLlama:7B and CodeLlama:13B achieve nearly identical RSR (10% vs 12.5% in baseline), with no significant gain from parameter scaling.
Description and BuggyLine are universally high-value (improving RSR by 7.5–10pp for all models); PDG and TestOutput only benefit high-capability models.
TestFile is low-value noise (reducing RSR by 2.5–5pp).
Avoided information: Independent TestFile (low-value noise, only used in combination with TestOutput for commercial models after redundancy cleaning).
Dataset Limitations: The study only uses the QuixBugs Python subset (40 cases), which is small—results may not generalize to large-scale projects, syntax errors.

Model Coverage Limitations: Only 6 models are tested, lacking coverage of emerging code-specific LLMs (e.g., CodeLlama 70B, StarCoder) and multilingual models—future studies should include more diverse models to verify the generalizability of the “triple dividend” framework.
